desc:
A region has n towns labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry roads[i] = [a, b, w] is a two-way road between towns a and b of length w.

For every unordered pair of different towns {i, j}, take the length of the shortest route between them. Return the sum of these values over all n(n - 1) / 2 pairs. If even one pair of towns cannot reach each other, return -1.

Example: with n = 3 and roads [[0,1,4],[1,2,3],[0,2,10]] the shortest distances are d(0,1) = 4, d(1,2) = 3 and d(0,2) = 4 + 3 = 7 (going through town 1 beats the direct road of 10), so the answer is 14.
constraints: roads[i] = [a, b, w] with 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b and 1 ≤ w ≤ 1,000
No two roads join the same pair of towns
hints: You need the distance between every pair of towns, not from a single source. With n up to 80, an O(n3) method is fine.
Let d[i][j] be the best known distance from i to j. Start with direct roads (0 on the diagonal, infinity elsewhere), then ask for each town k: is going through k better?

Floyd-Warshall: for k in 0..n-1, for all i, j, set d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]). The outer loop must be over the intermediate town k. Afterwards add up d[i][j] for i < j, or return -1 on the first infinity.
editorial: Floyd-Warshall solves the all-pairs problem by dynamic programming over the set of allowed intermediate towns. After processing towns 0..k, d[i][j] is the shortest distance from i to j using only those towns as stops in between. Allowing town k means a shortest route either avoids k (the old value) or passes through it once, splitting into i to k and k to j that only use earlier stops.

The three loops give O(n3) time and O(n2) space, which is about half a million steps for n = 80. Running Dijkstra from every town costs O(n · (E log n)) and is better on sparse graphs, but Floyd-Warshall is shorter to write and works unchanged when weights are negative. Sum the upper triangle only, because the graph is undirected and d[i][j] = d[j][i]. If any entry stays infinite the graph is disconnected and the answer is -1.
